name: Shiproom — the pre-flight check for your demo video
one_liner: Drop the screen recording you're about to post on X into Shiproom and, entirely in your browser, it scrubs every frame for things you didn't mean to show — API keys, customer names, Slack DMs, your email in the browser chrome, the unpaid-invoice banner — and hands back a timestamped "leak list" plus the same video with those boxes blurred.
problem: Every launch post on X right now is a 30-second screen recording (tonight's bookmarks alone: Ploid, Jev, Wonder, LFM3, Granted, skill-diet — six of ten posts are video). Those recordings are made in a hurry from a real working machine, so they carry whatever was on screen: a bearer token in a terminal, a customer's name in the CRM demo, a Slack notification sliding in, the user's own email in the browser profile avatar, an unmasked .env. Today the only defence is watching your own video twice at 0.5x and hoping, or paying for a video editor and manually dragging blur boxes. Most people just post and find out. The ones who notice afterwards delete the post and lose the launch momentum, or rotate a key in a panic.
target_customer: Indie builders, founders and devrel people who post demo videos on X, in Show HN threads, in Product Hunt galleries and in Loom links to customers. They hang out exactly where tonight's bookmarks come from: build-in-public X, r/LocalLLaMA, Indie Hackers, dev Discords. Free and open source; no buyer, this is a reputation project.
why_now: LFM3 shipped on 2026-10-27 with an ONNX build and a working WebGPU/Transformers.js space (https://huggingface.co/spaces/webml-community/LFM3-VL-2B-WebGPU), so a 2B vision-language model that can look at a frame and say "this is a Slack DM from a named person" now runs client-side at q4f16 (~1.69 GB) with no server and no upload (https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B-ONNX, https://docs.liquid.ai/deployment/on-device/onnx). Six months ago the only way to semantically review a video for leaks was to upload it to a cloud API — which is exactly the thing a privacy tool must not do. It also lands on a16z's security-agenda point that the attack surface now includes what employees ship themselves (https://www.a16z.news/p/the-new-security-agenda).
comparables: GitLab wrote up the general recipe (split video into frames, OCR, run secret patterns) but as internal pipeline work, not a tool anyone can use: https://about.gitlab.com/blog/how-to-detecting-secrets-in-video/. VideoLens has a hosted "video privacy analyzer" that reviews sampled frames — but it is a cloud upload and aimed at content review, not at a builder about to post a launch clip: https://videolens.io/video-privacy-analyzer. There are dozens of free still-image redactors (https://datablur.app/, https://folge.me/blur-screenshot, https://blur-face.com/) — all single screenshots, all manual boxes, none handle video or a timeline. kabir0st/automated-video-privacy-pipeline blurs faces in video locally, but only faces, and it's a Python pipeline not a page: https://github.com/kabir0st/automated-video-privacy-pipeline. Gitleaks gives the regex corpus for free: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks. Gap: nobody has the one-drop, zero-upload, video-timeline version aimed at the person about to hit Post.
market_note: No revenue intended — free and open source. Estimate only: the addressable crowd is the tens of thousands of people who post a product demo video in any given month across X, Show HN and Product Hunt. Willingness to pay is near zero for the scan; the plausible paid edge later is a team/CI version ("block the Loom before it leaves the org"), which is where a16z's security-agenda framing points.
risks: A regex-only version is trivially cloneable and the still-image redactors (datablur.app, folge.me) could add video in a weekend. The VLM pass may produce false positives that annoy more than they help — flagging a fake name in a seed-data demo as a customer leak makes the tool feel dumb fast. And a 1.69 GB first-load is a real bounce risk for a tool people try once on a whim; the OCR-only fast path has to be genuinely useful on its own or most visitors never see the clever part.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That the LFM3-VL pass adds enough over plain OCR+regex to be worth a 1.7 GB download — if the semantic findings (customer names, Slack DMs) are weak or hallucinated, the tool collapses into a regex scanner and loses its freshness and its wow. 2) That people will run a check on a video they already consider finished; this is a latent pain, nobody currently searches for this, so the launch post has to create the fear. 3) That WebCodecs frame sampling at 2fps on a 1-3 minute 1080p screen recording stays fast enough (under ~60s) on an average laptop with the VLM in the loop.
first_customers: The build-in-public cohort in tonight's bookmarks and their replies: @m9rcn, @shengkunye, @nicopreme, @yashsharma_f, @usewonder all posted video launches this week — DM each of them the scan of their own public video with the findings list. Then r/LocalLLaMA (the LFM3-WebGPU thread crowd), Show HN, and the Transformers.js/webml-community Discord, who reward anything that runs a new model fully client-side.
validation_test: This week: take 10 demo videos already public on X from launch posts, run the pipeline manually (sample frames, OCR, regex, eyeball), and count how many contain at least one real finding. Pass = 3 or more of 10 have something the author plainly didn't mean to show; that number becomes the launch post's hook. Fail = 0-1, in which case the pain is imaginary and this should be dropped rather than shipped.
build_plan: Stack: single static page, TypeScript, no backend. (1) Ingest: read the dropped .mp4/.mov with a <video> element + WebCodecs/canvas, sample 2 frames/sec into an OffscreenCanvas (cut ffmpeg.wasm — WebCodecs is enough for screen recordings). (2) Fast pass: Tesseract.js OCR each sampled frame, run the Gitleaks regex corpus plus email/phone/JWT/entropy checks over the words, keep each hit's bounding box and timestamp. (3) Smart pass: for frames that OCR flags, or every 10th frame, send the frame to LFM3-VL-2B via Transformers.js WebGPU with a fixed prompt ("list anything a stranger should not see: personal names, chat messages, account emails, billing info") — this catches the things regex can't, like a Slack DM or a real customer name. First load downloads ~1.7 GB once, cached; show a progress bar and let people run OCR-only while it loads. (4) Result screen: a timeline with red markers, a list of findings ("0:14 — AWS key in terminal", "0:22 — Slack DM from a named person"), each click-to-seek. (5) Export: re-render the video to canvas with the flagged boxes blurred and download it, plus a copyable "Clean ✅ / 3 things found" badge card. (6) Ship as a GitHub repo + Vercel static deploy. Cut for v1: audio/transcript scanning, face blur, mobile, long videos (cap at 3 minutes).
launch_post:
Half of X is launch videos recorded on a real laptop. Mine had an API key in frame for 4 seconds.

Shiproom: drop your demo video, it scrubs every frame for keys, emails, customer names and Slack DMs, then hands it back blurred.

100% in your browser. Nothing uploads. Open source.
reasoning: Tonight's bookmark set is overwhelmingly launch videos — six of ten posts are screen recordings shipped the same day they were made. That is the tell: the audience in these bookmarks produces exactly the artefact Shiproom checks, which makes distribution trivial (scan their own public videos and reply). It beat the other candidates on three counts. Against the skill/agent-tooling candidates (2, 10) it isn't a repeat: past ideas Shelf and Skillscope already own the SKILL.md-paste workflow for the same audience, and Shiproom's input (a video file), audience (anyone posting a demo) and output (a blurred file) share nothing with them. Against the people-data candidates (3) it avoids both the $2.50/lookup wall and the overlap with tonight's data-heavy venture. Against the pure-model toys (4, 5) it has a reason to exist after the novelty: you run it before every launch, not once. It also differs from tonight's venture pick Frailty entirely — different people, different problem, different workflow. could_grow is true because the obvious next step is a team version that gates Loom/Cap exports before they leave an org, which is the "employees shipping things themselves" surface a16z's CISO survey says is the fastest-growing 2027 priority. The honest ceiling is 7.6, not 9: shareability is the weak leg — people will share their findings, but a redacted video is by definition something you share *instead of* the scan, and I could not find evidence of similar scans spreading before. I did not inflate it.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Frailty — provider-side Medicaid medically-frail exemption packets for CCBHCs/OTPs. PICK. Dated deadline, named buyer, confirmed unserved layer between member navigators and state eligibility engines.
2. Ploid-powered "who is this person really" KYC/KYA layer for agent payments (from @m9rcn + a16z KYA big idea). Dropped at screen — infrastructure play, crowded with funded identity vendors, no specific buyer with a budget line the builder could reach.
3. Lead-waterfall cost governor for RevOps (from @shengkunye's Jev post): route enrichment across Apollo/Clay/PDL and pay per kept lead. Dropped at screen — Jev itself is this, open source and free; cloning it fails the no-thin-variation rule.
4. Outbound-reply triage and spam-suppression layer for SMBs being carpet-bombed by Explee-style AI prospecting. Dropped at screen — buyer is the victim, not a budget holder; my search for expressed complaints returned nothing usable.
5. "AI laggard" token-and-adoption allocator for Heads of AI (from @businessbarista). Dropped at screen — crowded with Copilot adoption/shelfware analytics vendors (CloudNuro, LicenseIQ, VisualSP), and the honest version is an HR layoff tool the builder would not want to sell.
6. Deal Bot for the mid-market: non-standard contract terms detection and exception routing (from @bot's Shared Bots post). Finalist, lost. Real workflow, but CPQ/deal-desk incumbents (Salesforce Revenue Cloud, DealHub, Conga, Salesbricks) already route non-standard terms for exactly this buyer at a fair price; no confirmable gap and no deadline.
7. Internal AI-agent permission evidence pack for mid-market CISOs facing SOC 2 (from a16z's CISO survey: 46% worried about agents exceeding permissions, 45% plan to buy within 12 months). Finalist, lost. Strong timing and budget, but the "Okta + SailPoint for agents" category is already forming with funded entrants, and it is too close to past ideas Proofline and Holdroom in buyer and workflow.
8. On-device vertical inspection model packaging for field techs, riding LFM3's 1-GPU fine-tune and NPU targets. Dropped at screen — a capability in search of a buyer; the builder would be selling model ops to people who buy outcomes.
9. Permit correction-letter drafter for small building departments (YC "AI for City Hall"). Dropped at screen — CivCheck is already piloting with Honolulu and Seattle, Clariti distributes it, and municipal sales cycles are far too slow for an evenings-and-weekends founder to reach a first sale.
10. Hours-proof concierge for gig and shift workers subject to the same 2027 rule. Dropped at screen — consumer-side, no payer, and research confirmed employers have no new reporting duty, so there is no B2B hook.

PROJECT
1. Shiproom — pre-post leak scan for demo videos, fully in-browser with LFM3-VL + OCR. PICK: only candidate with a real (if latent) problem, a brand-new capability behind it, and an output that is both useful and postable.
2. Skill Diet Scoreboard — paste a SKILL.md, see its token cost and what a slimmed version would save. DROPPED AT SCREEN: too close to past ideas Shelf and Skillscope (same audience, same paste-a-SKILL.md workflow), and skill-diet itself already does the real version.
3. "What your agent sees" — paste your handle, Ploid/public-web data assembled into a profile card. DROPPED AT SCREEN: Ploid is $2.50 per person report with no usable free tier, and Whitebridge.ai plus a shelf of OSINT tools already do this; also creepy-adjacent and overlaps the venture's people-data theme.
4. Omni Memo — hum/talk at LFM3-Omni-2B in the browser, get structured typed output. DROPPED AT SCREEN: Omni's ONNX browser path isn't demonstrated yet (only VL has a working WebGPU space), so buildability was a coin flip.
5. Decision Desk — d1-2B typed decisions with calibrated probabilities over a pasted CSV. DROPPED AT SCREEN: genuinely fresh (YC's vertical-foundation-models signal points right at it) but the output is a probability table — nothing anyone screenshots, and no hosted free endpoint confirmed.
6. Laggard Mirror — paste your week's AI usage, see where you sit on the "10% do 90%" power law. DROPPED: the data is self-reported, so the output is fiction; also mean-spirited.
7. Patent-style exploded diagram generator — rejected immediately as a repeat of past ideas Figures and Partsy.
8. Bookmark Shelf — your X bookmarks rendered as a browsable shelf. DROPPED: Granted (@yashsharma_f) is literally this week's bookmark-agent launch; building a thin neighbour of a bookmarked project is against the brief.
9. Changelog Tide — weekly diff of what the top 50 open models can now do in-browser. DROPPED AT SCREEN: good reason to return, but it's a newsletter with a UI; no personal input, nothing to post.
10. Caption Loop — real-time webcam captioning with LFM3-VL WebGPU. DROPPED: the webml-community space and the r/LocalLLaMA video-captioning demo already exist; cloning a published demo.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): Web Summary on ploid.com (confirmed real pricing — $200/mo Growth, 1,000 credits, 25 credits for a deep person lookup — which killed the "people data is now cents" framing as a venture angle for this builder); on a16z's New Security Agenda (gave real CISO numbers: 46% fear agents exceeding permissions, 45% plan to buy internal-agent security within 12 months, 87% expect budget growth — this is what elevated candidate 7 to finalist); on Explee (confirmed $0.04/email pay-as-you-go, which showed how commoditised AI outbound already is and sank candidates 3 and 4).

Screening pot (6/6): agentic identity/NHI governance (found the "Okta + SailPoint for agents" category already forming); city permitting (found CivCheck live in Honolulu and piloted in Seattle, distributed by Clariti — killed candidate 9); Copilot adoption/shelfware (found CloudNuro, LicenseIQ, VisualSP — killed candidate 5); GDPR/data-broker angle (returned nothing usable); deal desk / CPQ (found DealHub, Conga, Salesbricks, Salesforce all routing non-standard terms — demoted candidate 6); benefits income verification (found Plaid Income, SteadyIQ, Argyle, Code for America — pushed me off the income-verification wedge and toward exemptions).

Deep research pot (12/12): spent almost entirely on the Medicaid work-requirement finalist. Established the deadline and scale (KFF tracker, CBO ~5.3M more uninsured by 2034, Urban ~3.1M fewer enrollees year one, Nebraska/Montana/Arkansas/Iowa already moving); mapped the vendor landscape on both ends (Fortuna Health $22M a16z-backed, Healthy Together, Vimo, Centauri, Ushur, mPulse, Pointcare, Relay, Deloitte via KFF) and confirmed none sells the provider-side clinical packet; found the CMS IFR's two-part medically-frail test and the three-tier framework; found Kentucky's MACE-200 and the 30-day cure process; found SHVS's 8 Oct 2026 roadmap telling states to publish standardised provider attestation forms; found an independent analyst explicitly naming the clinician-review tier as unbuilt. Two calls were spent trying and failing to get clinic-level burden and revenue numbers — that failure is why pain stayed at 8.

Sharpening pot (5/5): sized the behavioural-health buyer (495 CCBHCs / ~3M clients; 2,112 OTPs, >600k patients/yr, ~75% Medicaid; Medicare OTP weekly methadone bundle $277.29; KFF $1,609 Medicaid revenue per health-centre patient/yr), checked behavioural-health SaaS price points ($35-$150 per clinician per month, $0.38/claim) to see whether a per-clinic price is normal, and probed multi-state form availability (confirmed Kentucky, could not confirm Montana/Nebraska/Iowa/Indiana — which is why v1 is one state).

Investor signals weighed: YC [latest] "Plaid for Government Benefits" (Alströmer) aimed me at benefits paperwork and I took the narrow provider-side wedge inside it rather than the signal itself; YC [latest] "AI for City Hall" produced candidate 9, killed by CivCheck; YC [latest] "The $15-an-Hour Expert" shaped the product's form (a non-specialist assembling a packet a clinician signs); a16z [latest] "Vertical AI ... to multiplayer" and "AI reinforces business models" supported the provider-revenue framing; a16z's CISO post produced candidate 7. The signals raised timing, not pain or market_pull — those rest on the CMS rule and the state forms I verified myself.
Sharpening (7.4 to 8): Round 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6) and market_pull (6). The original finalist was a generic "Medicaid work-requirement compliance helper for FQHCs and CBOs". Research showed that lane is crowded on both ends: Fortuna Health ($22M, a16z Bio+Health) owns member navigation; Healthy Together and Vimo ship member/state hour-logging and exemption screening (CBPP vendor landscape); Centauri, Ushur, mPulse, Pointcare own payer-side retention outreach. Change to the idea: drop member navigation entirely and move the wedge to the one step none of them touch — the clinician-signed medically-frail packet built from the chart. Evidence found: CMS's IFR makes medical frailty a two-part functional test, not a diagnosis lookup; an independent analyst states the clinician-review tier is unserved and frames it as a layer to sell alongside Fortuna rather than against it; my search for a provider-side exemption documentation vendor returned none. gap 6 → 8, market_pull 6 → 7 (buyer named, but I still have no signed price).

Round 2 — weakest remaining: market_pull (7) and wedge (6). Change: narrow the buyer from "FQHCs and CBOs" to safety-net behavioural health — CCBHCs and OTPs — because their patients map almost one-to-one onto the SUD/SMI frailty categories, they have a single ops/compliance buyer, and the revenue-at-risk argument is sharp. Then narrow the first version to one state with a published provider form. Evidence found: Kentucky already publishes MACE-200 with a provider-signature version and accepts a letterhead attestation; SHVS's 8 Oct 2026 roadmap directs non-self-attestation states to finalise standardised provider attestation forms; SAMHSA lists 2,112 OTPs (~600k patients/yr) and the National Council 495 CCBHCs; behavioural health clinics already buy $35-$150/clinician/month add-ons, so a per-clinic price is normal. What did NOT survive: I could not find any measured volume of letter requests hitting clinics, any clinic staffing data for this task, or a behavioural-health-specific revenue-per-lost-patient figure — so pain stays at 8 (workaround clearly exists and is manual, but no hours/cost numbers) and wedge rises only to 7, because v1 needs state-specific rule encoding and a clinician trust bar, not a weekend. market_pull 7 held (named role, known price points, but no confirmed buyer). Average before sharpening 7.4 → after 8.0.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): Perplexity on LFM3 open weights and browser viability; on nicobailon/skill-diet (which killed candidate 2 — the real tool already does the evaluation loop properly, so a web clone would be worse); on ploid.com pricing, which surfaced the $2.50-per-person-report wall and killed candidate 3. Screening pot (5/5): one search each on SKILL.md token-audit tools (found skill-diet neighbours and ksred/firecrawl commentary — crowded), LFM3 browser support (found the webml-community WebGPU space, which both confirmed the capability and killed candidate 10 as a clone), digital-footprint tools (Whitebridge.ai and a pile of OSINT agents — crowded), AI-sales-agent data tools (saturated), and LFM3-Omni browser support (no demonstrated ONNX browser path yet — killed candidate 4). Deep research (8/8): d1-2B economics and hosting (no confirmed free hosted tier → candidate 5 out); two searches on still-image redaction, which found a dozen free tools (datablur.app, folge.me, blur-face.com) and forced the idea off screenshots and onto video, where nothing free and local exists; searches for video secret-detection, which turned up GitLab's pipeline writeup and hosted VideoLens as the only prior art; frame-extraction feasibility (WebCodecs/ffmpeg.wasm, Simon Willison's wasm tools as precedent); and the Tesseract.js + Gitleaks dependency check. What changed: the whole idea moved from "scan a screenshot" (dead, crowded) to "scan the video you're about to post" (open), and the architecture split into a cheap regex pass plus a selective model pass. Sharpening pot (4/4): the "before you post" searches, the build-in-public leak-anecdote searches (which returned general API-key-leak stories but no X-specific evidence — this is why pain_type is latent, not expressed, and why shareability stayed at 7), VideoLens pricing/alternatives, and the Tesseract/Gitleaks confirmation. Not checked and therefore capped: whether LFM3-VL's semantic findings on real screen-recording frames are accurate enough to trust — that is the riskiest assumption and the validation test targets it.
Sharpening (7.2 to 7.6): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (6.5 → 7.5). Problem: a one-shot "scan my video" is a toy you use once. Change to the idea: made the unit of work the launch itself rather than the file — the result screen ends in an exportable clean video plus a "Clean ✅ / N found" badge, so the tool becomes a step in a recurring ritual (every demo video, every launch) rather than a curiosity. Research (searches for a "before you post" demo-video checker, and for existing frame-by-frame privacy scrubbers) found only hosted/cloud VideoLens (https://videolens.io/video-privacy-analyzer), an internal GitLab pipeline writeup (https://about.gitlab.com/blog/how-to-detecting-secrets-in-video/) and a face-only Python pipeline (https://github.com/kabir0st/automated-video-privacy-pipeline) — nothing occupying the repeat-use, zero-upload slot. Score before 7.2, after 7.4.
Round 2 — weak criterion: buildability (7 → 8). Problem: "run a VLM over every frame of a video in the browser" was an unchecked claim and would be slow. Change to the idea: split into a fast OCR+Gitleaks-regex pass that runs immediately and a selective LFM3-VL pass only on flagged/sampled frames, with the model download non-blocking. Research confirmed every dependency: Tesseract.js is pure-JS in-browser OCR (https://tesseract.projectnaptha.com/), the Gitleaks regex corpus is open (https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks), and LFM3-VL-2B-ONNX q4f16 is ~1.69 GB and runs via Transformers.js v4.3.2+ with a live WebGPU space (https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B-ONNX, https://huggingface.co/spaces/webml-community/LFM3-VL-2B-WebGPU). Freshness held but capped at 7.5 rather than 9, because the honest core (OCR + regex over frames) has been possible for years and only the semantic pass is new; the LFM Open License also has a commercial-use limitation I could not fully clear, which is fine for a free OSS tool but worth noting. Score before 7.4, after 7.6.
prototype_summary: Shiproom is a browser-local pre-flight scanner that finds and blurs secrets, personal data and customer names visible in a demo video before you post it.
